claims.notes: THE TOWN'S TRAFFIC, IN THE POSTMASTER'S OWN TABLE. Four mails serve Chicago in February 1834 — Eastern, Western, Northern and Southern — and all four ARRIVE on a Tuesday or a Wednesday and LEAVE on a Thursday or a Saturday, at six or eight in the morning. For a reconstruction this is a rhythm, not a decoration: the post office is a crowded room twice a week and empty the rest of it, and the roads into town carry a mail on named days. It also fixes the head of the stage system the next issue advertises in full (1834-02-18, claim c002 there), where the Detroit mail's connection at Chicago is the thing the timetable is built around. Hogan signs as postmaster here, on the January letter list (1834-02-04, claim c013 there) and on the scene-date issue.

claims.notes: THE ACADEMY'S FIRST QUARTER ENDS, WHICH DATES ITS OPENING. The paper attended the examination the card of 1834-02-04 advertised (claim c004 there) and calls it 'the termination of [its] first quarter' — so the Chicago Academy opened about November 1833 and was a going school, teaching geography, astronomy and mathematics to a whole school of pupils, twenty months before the scene date. The subjects are the only curriculum this corpus has for it before the second term advertisement of 1834-02-25 (claim c001 there). The middle of the notice is unreadable and is left inside its bracket.

claims.notes: A DATED, PERISHABLE STOCK. Peter Cohen's standing card in this same issue sets him at 'EAST END OF SOUTH WATER-STREET' (1834-02-04 page 3 column 6 line 2761), which is the address the scene-date issue and the first issue both carry, so the street is taken from him and not from this line. What this advertisement adds is a DATE: fresh butter in quantity, advertised the day the paper went to press in the middle of February, which is a town being supplied from the country by sleigh and not by the lake. The quantity is cut and is not supplied.

entities.role: merchant winding up his Chicago business

claims.notes: RULING 3'S VETO, PRINTED. A Chicago merchant has SOLD OUT HIS STOCK and is leaving for New-York as soon as his accounts are settled — so this business does NOT stand at the scene date, and the claim carries `contradicts` so the compiler computes `built_at_scene_date: false` rather than a reader asserting it. This is the first business in the corpus to be closed by its own notice. THE SAME MAN IS ON THE JANUARY LETTER LIST five weeks earlier — the Democrat's post-office column of 1834-02-04 sets '[O]. T. Breed' among the B's (claim c013 there, line 2883) — which is what a man expects who has letters waiting and is about to leave. The forename initials are cut in the list and printed here, and the reading is bracketed in both because 'O. T.' is read off a damaged line.

claims.notes: A DOCUMENTED STOREFRONT ON A NAMED CORNER, twenty months before the scene date. The corner of LaSalle and South Water is the address the gazetteer already carries for P. F. W. Peck out of the 1835 papers; this is the same corner in February 1834, which is what a survival argument needs — the same man, the same corner, seventeen months apart, with no notice between them moving him. The trade is a general store: dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes and hats. Peck also reports the paper's weekly prices current (1834-02-04, claim c011 there).

claims.notes: THE FIRM THE STREET IS MEASURED FROM. Brewster, Hogan & Co. is the anchor Collins & Caton's office is placed against in the same month — 'one door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co., South Water street' (1834-02-04, claim c006 there) — so the firm is ON South Water Street, and the street is taken from that cross-reference rather than from this card, which gives no address at all. The placement class is `street_only` for exactly that reason: the paper puts them on a street and not at a point. The quantity of barrels and the bushels of hickory nuts beside them are cut in every printing this month and are not supplied.
